evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: An institution fully decentralized in its operational protocol without a centralized arbitration mechanism for resolving protocol disputes]

[PATH:empirical] Case studies of DAO governance failures (e.g., The DAO hack, MakerDAO emergency shutdowns, Solend whale intervention) - documented in blockchain forensics reports and academic analyses. — These real-world instances provide direct evidence of whether fully decentralized protocols can resolve disputes without centralized arbitration, or whether such mechanisms were ultimately required.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal game-theoretic models of decentralized consensus and dispute resolution (e.g., Schelling points, futarchy, or token-curated registries) as published in journals like 'Journal of Economic Theory' or 'Distributed Computing'. — These models can prove whether it is logically possible for a protocol to remain fully decentralized while achieving stable resolution of disputes without any central authority, testing the hypothesis under idealized conditions.

[PATH:literature] Comparative literature review of governance structures in blockchain protocols (e.g., Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tezos, Polkadot) from 'Communications of the ACM' or 'Ledger' journal. — Synthesizing existing empirical and theoretical findings across multiple protocols can reveal patterns about the necessity or absence of centralized arbitration in truly decentralized operational protocols.

qualifier.temporal: since the advent of blockchain-based governance models (circa 2009)
